title: Resource Contention in Production

sections.title: Synchronous Dependencies on the Request Path
Shared Pools and Fleet-Wide Session Limits
Open-Loop Load Testing and Flag Rollback

html:
Much of your day as an engineer is spent changing an application that already serves customers. A request arrives in the team’s backlog. The product manager wants a “Recommended for you” row on every product page, because customers who see related items tend to buy more of them. Another team already runs a Recommendation Service for the home page, so the change seems trivial. You add one call to the product-page handler, write a test with a stubbed response, open a pull request, and the reviewer approves it the same afternoon.

Your test with the stubbed response checked only the handler’s logic. The stub replied in a fraction of a millisecond and touched no database, so the test measured nothing about the work behind the production service. In production, every product page would send a request to Recommendation Service, and every one of those requests would borrow a database connection from a pool that the home page and checkout were already using. The reviewer had no reason to examine that pool, because the pull request contained no code that touched it.

That was the situation at Baodium when the product-page team added personalized recommendations. The integration returned correct suggestions in testing, but the release plan contained no estimate of how many extra lookups the shared database would receive. The handler also waited for recommendations before returning the product, even though a customer could browse and buy without them.

Synchronous Dependencies on the Request Path

Before the change, Product Page Service fetched product details from Catalog Service and used them to build the response (Figure Figure).

The new handler added a second call and waited for it before building the page.

def get_product_page(user_id, product_id):
    product = catalog_service.fetch(product_id)
    recs = recommendation_service.get(user_id, product_id)
    return build_response(product, recs)

Let’s look at the order of those three lines. The recommendation call sits between fetching the product and building the response, so a slow lookup delays the whole page. The product manager had asked for personalization as an addition to the page, yet the code made every page wait for it. An optional feature had become a required one. No configuration file or design document recorded that decision, because it existed only in the order of three lines of code, and code review focused on whether those lines were correct.

The team enabled the feature for one percent of eligible customers. A feature-flag service published the rollout percentage, and each Product Page instance checked the flag before making the recommendation call.1 One percent of customers does not necessarily mean one percent of page requests, because some customers browse far more than others, and the release owner was watching the customer percentage rather than lookup rates. The percentage went up in stages. For the first few stages, the latency dashboard showed no change. Then the slowest pages began to take longer while the median barely changed, and seventeen minutes after the first increase, a customer-facing latency alert fired.

Diagnosing Connection-Pool Saturation

The on-call engineer first examined the recommendation queries. Their execution times were close to the measurements taken before the release, which made slow Structured Query Language (SQL) statements an unlikely explanation for the page delays. It did not rule out every database problem, since lock waits or a few slow queries can hide inside an average, but it sent the investigation to the part of the request that happens before a query runs.

That part is the connection pool. Opening a database connection involves a network handshake and authentication, which is too slow to repeat for every request, so an application maintains open connections and lends one to each request while it talks to the database. The set of connections is the connection pool. Some pools open their connections at startup, and others create them on demand, but both enforce a configured maximum. A bank branch with forty tellers works the same way. Each transaction might take only a minute, but a customer who arrives when every teller is busy waits in line before the transaction can even start, and the line, rather than the transaction, makes the visit slow.

Each Recommendation Service instance allowed at most 40 connections. The engineer pulled up the pool’s readout from an affected instance (Listing Listing).2

assigned_connections    40
idle_connections        0
pending_acquisitions    80
acquire_p99             600 ms
query_p99               near baseline
occupancy_mean          70 ms

All 40 connections were assigned, and another 80 requests were waiting to acquire one. The acquire_p99 line is the 99th percentile, often written p99. It means that 99 percent of acquisitions finished within 600 milliseconds and the slowest one percent took longer, so a meaningful share of requests waited more than half a second before their SQL even started. Because they had not reached the database yet, their wait never appeared in the query timings, which is why those timings alone had given no warning. The pages were slow because their recommendation calls were queuing for a connection.

Acquisition, Execution, and Occupancy

The readout was useful because the service measured three intervals separately. Acquisition is the time a request spends waiting to receive a connection. Execution is the time a single SQL statement takes once it runs. Occupancy is the whole time a request has the connection before returning it, including any work it does between statements.

Each combination of these numbers sends an investigation in a different direction. Long acquisition with normal execution means requests are queuing for the pool, so the engineers turn to demand, bursts, and how long each request occupies its connection. Fast acquisition with slow execution directs attention to the database itself, its query plans, locks, and disk. Had the team recorded only total request time, both situations would have produced the same graph, and the first fix most people reach for, tuning the queries, would have left the queue in place. Chapter 8 shows how to collect these measurements across a whole request path, including the attempts that time out before they receive a connection.

Shared Pools and Fleet-Wide Session Limits

Product pages produced most of the new lookups, but home-page and checkout requests drew from the same pool and waited in the same line. That is how an optional feature on the product page began to slow checkout, the page the business could least afford to slow.

Two fixes came up during the incident call. A bigger pool would let more lookups run concurrently, and more Recommendation Service instances would spread the traffic. Both sound reasonable, and both open more database sessions. Each instance has its own pool, so twenty instances allowed forty connections each could open 800 sessions against one PostgreSQL server. Two separate limits sit behind that number. PostgreSQL caps the number of sessions it will accept, and, independently, the server has a limited amount of central processing unit (CPU) time, memory, and disk to run the queries those sessions send. A database that accepts 800 sessions may still slow down badly when 800 queries run concurrently. The engineers on the call did not know how much of either limit had been allocated to Recommendation Service, so raising the pool size or the number of instances risked turning a slow feature into a database outage.

Decision review

Which mitigation restores the required page?

Personalization has reached full exposure. The pool has 40 assigned connections, 80 pending acquisitions, and an acquisition p99 of 600 ms. SQL latency is near baseline. The release owner can disable personalization, increase the connection pool, or add replicas.

Increase each pool from 40 to 80 connections.

Add four Recommendation Service replicas.

Disable personalization while the team investigates.

The third option removes the optional demand without introducing more sessions on a database whose limits have not been tested at that level. Increasing pool size or replica total could be appropriate later, after the database’s session limit and throughput have been measured. The team disabled personalization, then designed a bounded lookup and measured both page completion and recommendation delivery during its next rollout.

Optional Dependencies With Bounded Admission

Turning the flag off brought product pages back, but the product manager still wanted the feature. Before comparing designs, the team wrote down what the feature had to deliver. A product page must always return the product within its latency objective. Recommendations should appear on at least 95 percent of eligible pages during peak traffic, and the page should never wait in a queue for them. The delivery target was the requirement that ruled designs out. A design that protected latency by dropping recommendations on most pages would meet the latency objective and still fail the product goal.

With those requirements written down, the team compared three designs (Table Table).

Parallel calls would shorten the page but leave the database load unchanged, which was the cause of the incident. Precomputation would remove most live queries, and Chapter 5 examines that option in detail, but it needed a new refresh pipeline and storage that the team could not build in time for the next promotion. A bounded lookup retained the live design and capped both how many lookups each instance could run and how long the page would wait.3 The open question was whether those caps could still deliver recommendations on 95 percent of pages, and only a load test could settle that.

Choosing the Limits

Two settings define the bounded lookup, and the team derived each one from a measurement. The concurrency limit came from the database side. The database team allocated Recommendation Service a share of sessions and query capacity, and dividing that share across the expected number of instances, with room for one instance to fail, gave each Product Page instance 16 concurrent recommendation calls. The time budget came from the page side. The product page had a latency objective, building and sending the response took a measured slice of it, and the time left over for optional work was about 150 milliseconds. Listing Listing records both settings where the handler can read them.

import threading

# From the tested per-instance allocation (Chapter 2).
REC_CONCURRENCY = 16
# Optional-work share of the page latency objective.
REC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 0.15
# Time reserved for building and sending the response.
RENDER_RESERVE_SECONDS = 0.05

rec_slots = threading.BoundedSemaphore(REC_CONCURRENCY)
def page(user_id, product_id, deadline):
    product = catalog_service.fetch(product_id)
    budget = min(REC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
                 deadline.remaining_seconds() - RENDER_RESERVE_SECONDS)
    if budget <= 0 or not rec_slots.acquire(blocking=False):
        metrics.rec_skipped.inc()
        return build_response(product, recommendations=[])
    try:
        recs = recommendation_service.get(
            user_id, product_id, timeout=budget)
    except (TimeoutError, ServiceUnavailable):
        metrics.rec_failed.inc()
        recs = []
    finally:
        rec_slots.release()
    return build_response(product, recommendations=recs)

Let’s read the handler from top to bottom. It fetches the product first, because the page is useless without it. It then works out how much time it can spend on recommendations, which is the smaller of the fixed budget and whatever is left of the page’s deadline after setting aside time to build the response. If no time is left, or all 16 slots are in use, the page goes out without a recommendation row, and a counter records the skip. That is how a busy Recommendation Service stops building a queue inside the product page. When a slot is free, the call runs with the computed budget, and a timeout or an unavailable service produces an empty row and a counter increment rather than an error page. The finally block returns the slot whatever happens, so a failed call cannot leak capacity.

The handler catches only the failures the team expected, a timeout and an unavailable service. Any other exception, such as a bug in the recommendation client, still reaches the application’s error handling and shows up in the error rate, where an engineer will see it. Catching every exception would hide defects behind an empty row.

Before you copy this pattern, there are two limitations to know about. When the handler stops waiting, Recommendation Service may still be working on the request, so the caller’s timeout does not by itself free a database connection. And rec_slots limits one instance. Sixteen slots on each of twenty instances still allow 320 lookups across the fleet, so the per-instance number is only safe because it was derived from the fleet allocation. Chapter 4 covers deadlines and cancellation, and Chapter 9 turns per-instance limits into limits shared across a fleet.

Open-Loop Load Testing and Flag Rollback

The one-percent stage of the first rollout had sent too little traffic to reveal the pool limit, so before raising exposure again the team ran a load test at the expected peak rate. They used an open-loop test, which sends new requests on a fixed schedule however slowly the service responds. A test that waits for each response before sending the next one lowers its own load as the service slows, so it can hide the overload it is meant to find.4 Chapter 2 explains how to read the results of such a test and turn them into an admission limit.

The test ran at peak traffic, with uneven routing between instances, and again with one instance removed. In the worst case, product pages met their latency objective, connection acquisition was under ten milliseconds, and recommendations appeared on 97 percent of eligible pages, above the 95 percent target. Those results approved the two settings in Listing Listing and a rollout plan that raised exposure in stages, with the release owner watching recommendation lookups per instance rather than customer percentages.

The team also rehearsed turning the feature off. A flag change takes effect only after every instance has received the new setting, and requests already waiting for connections still finish or time out. The rehearsal measured both delays, so the release owner knew how long relief would take if the flag had to be switched off during another incident. Chapter 10 turns observations like these into release gates.

Summary

If you take one lesson from this chapter, make it this one. Every call you add to a request path borrows something that other requests also need, and the review that approves the code rarely shows what that is. Think back to the feature request that started the chapter. The developer added a recommendation call, tested its response, and released a feature the product team wanted. What the review missed was the extra demand the call would place on a database pool that checkout and the home page already depended on.

The investigation also showed how much depends on measuring the right part of a request. The SQL queries were completing as fast as they had before the release, while requests spent their time waiting for a connection. Once the engineers knew where the delay occurred, they could write down what the page truly needed, compare designs against those requirements, and choose limits that came from measurements of the database and the page budget.

You will meet the same decision when you add an entitlement check to a SaaS application, call an external fraud service, or fetch profile data from another team’s API. Each new call needs to fit within the resources the application already shares and the promises it already makes to its users. Here, the team discovered the problem in production. Chapter 2 takes us back to the design review, where we can estimate that demand before the change is released.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The live lookup can meet the page-latency objective and the recommendation-delivery target at a tested per-instance attempt rate.
Condition that tests it & Increasing feature exposure increases recommendation calls per instance.
Constraint or invariant & Per-instance connection pools share one database. The resource budget includes existing callers and the new product-page workload.
Evidence and uncertainty & The initial canary used a small fraction of the connection demand expected at full exposure. Acquisition waits increased when all connections were assigned.

Still unknown: the acceptable per-instance attempt rate under uneven routing, longer occupancy, or the loss of a service instance.
Signal and evaluation window & Compare connection acquisition, occupancy, and page latency with the pre-release baseline at each exposure step.
Control and decision & Limit exposure to the validated range. Reconsider live computation if recommendation delivery misses its target at that rate.
Owner and review trigger & The Recommendation Service owner provides load-test and recovery results. The release owner approves exposure against the recorded thresholds. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.

  1. LaunchDarkly and Unleash are examples of feature-flag systems. Chapter 10 shows how a flag selects a rollout cohort, how a new setting reaches every instance, and how a flag is disabled during an incident.↩︎

  2. A readout here means a point-in-time snapshot of the pool’s own counters and timings, as reported by the connection-pool library’s metrics or diagnostic endpoint. Field names differ between libraries, so the labels in this example are illustrative.↩︎

  3. A bounded lookup is a dependency call with two limits, a time budget that bounds how long the caller waits and an admission limit that bounds how many calls may be in flight concurrently. Chapter 4 discusses what happens when the caller stops waiting but the remote work carries on.↩︎

  4. In k6, the constant-arrival-rate executor schedules iterations at a fixed rate. Its dropped_iterations metric reports iterations that could not start.↩︎
